title: School Notebooks 5-pack

drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%)
drivers.evidence: Two prior weeks with same price saw no lift (2026-09-28, 2026-10-05), median x0.91 vs baseline; no uplift seen at higher price, suggesting demand is price-sensitive.

drivers.name: Competitor store opening across the street
drivers.evidence: No prior data on this event type; however, new competitor presence typically reduces demand. Noise-adjusted effect from similar events is uncertain, but plausible downside. Shrink toward 1.0 due to low evidence count.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median of 7.6 is elevated by recent back-to-school seasonality, but the target week is 5 weeks post-season, so that trend has likely faded. The price increased 2.3% to $9.03, which is above regular price. Past price increases (e.g., 2026-09-28, 2026-10-05) saw no lift, and a 30% off promo in April had a strong lift (x2.86), but the current price is higher. A competitor opening across the street is a downside driver: no prior data on such an event, but a new competitor likely reduces demand. The classical model suggests no uplift, consistent with weak past price effects. Evidence is thin but directional: price increase and new competitor imply a modest demand drop. Shrink toward 1.0. No promotion or event.

brief:
PRODUCT: School Notebooks 5-pack | category Office | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-15 (5 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 9.03 (+2.3% vs regular price 8.83)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 7.6 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 35.7 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 23.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-64% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
